title: Firewall Management with ufw
markdown:
# Firewall Management with `ufw`

When a server is exposed to the internet, **every open port is a potential attack surface**. Without a firewall, anyone on the internet can attempt to connect to any service running on your server — whether you intended them to or not.

A firewall sits in front of your server and acts like a **security guard at the entrance**. It inspects every incoming connection and decides: is this allowed, or should it be blocked?

On Ubuntu, the recommended tool for this is **`ufw` (Uncomplicated Firewall)**. It is a user-friendly frontend for `iptables` — replacing hundreds of low-level commands with short, readable instructions.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/ufw-01.svg)

`ufw` controls two things:

- **Default policy** — what happens to traffic that matches no rule (allow or deny everything by default)
- **Explicit rules** — specific instructions to allow or deny particular ports, protocols, or IP addresses

## What You Will Learn

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Check `ufw` status and read its current ruleset
- Set default policies for incoming and outgoing traffic
- Allow and deny traffic by port, protocol, IP address, and service name
- Use `ufw`'s application profiles to manage rules by service name
- Delete and reset rules safely

## The Scenario: Securing a New Application Server

The `Poridhi.io` platform team has deployed a new application server with three services running on it. Your job is to configure the firewall so that:

- Administrators can always SSH into the server
- The web application is reachable by everyone
- The monitoring tool is only reachable from inside the internal network
- All other traffic is blocked by default

| Port | Service | Who Can Access It |
|------|---------|-------------------|
| `22` | SSH (remote admin access) | Everyone |
| `8080` | Web application | Everyone |
| `9090` | Internal monitoring endpoint | Only `100.84.0.0/16` (internal network) |
| All others | — | Nobody (blocked by default) |

> **Critical safety rule:** Always allow SSH (`port 22`) **before** setting a default `deny` incoming policy. If you reverse the order, the firewall activates and immediately drops all incoming traffic — including your own SSH session, locking you out permanently. In the Poridhi lab environment, your session runs through a WireGuard VPN, so both port `22` and the VPN tunnel must remain open at all times.

## Part 1: Understanding How `ufw` Works

Before touching any commands, it helps to understand the logic behind how `ufw` makes decisions.

### How Rules Are Evaluated

Every time a connection arrives at your server, `ufw` checks it against your rules **one by one, from top to bottom**. The moment it finds a matching rule, it applies that rule's action and stops checking. If no rule matches, the **default policy** is used.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/ufw-02.svg)

**This order is critical.** If you put a broad `DENY ALL` rule before a specific `ALLOW SSH` rule, SSH gets blocked before it ever reaches the allow rule.

### Types of Rules You Can Write

| Rule Type | Example Command | What It Does |
|-----------|----------------|--------------|
| Allow by port | `ufw allow 22` | Allow all traffic on port 22 (TCP + UDP) |
| Allow by port + protocol | `ufw allow 22/tcp` | Allow only TCP traffic on port 22 |
| Allow by service name | `ufw allow ssh` | Same as `22/tcp`, uses `/etc/services` for the mapping |
| Allow from a subnet | `ufw allow from 100.84.0.0/16` | Allow all traffic from that IP range |
| Allow subnet to specific port | `ufw allow from 100.84.0.0/16 to any port 9090` | Allow that subnet, but only to port 9090 |
| Deny a port | `ufw deny 23` | Block all traffic on port 23 |

## Part 2: Checking Your Current Firewall State

Before making any changes, always check the current state first. This gives you a baseline and helps you avoid surprises.

### Step 1: Install Required Tools

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y ufw netcat-openbsd telnet
```

- `ufw` is the firewall tool (usually pre-installed on Ubuntu)
- `netcat-openbsd` gives us the `nc` command, which we'll use to simulate the monitoring service and test blocked connections
- `telnet` gives us the `telnet` command, which we'll use to test blocked connections

### Step 2: Check Whether `ufw` Is Active

```bash
sudo ufw status verbose
```

On a fresh Poridhi lab VM, `ufw` is **inactive** by default:

```bash
Status: inactive
```

This means no firewall rules are being enforced yet — all traffic flows freely. This is the expected starting point.

### Step 3: Check for Any Pre-Configured Rules

```bash
sudo ufw show added
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image.png)

This lists any rules that have been written but not yet applied (because `ufw` is still inactive). On a fresh VM, this returns nothing.

> **Note:** Do not modify anything in this part. This is observation only.

## Part 3: Setting Up the Lab Environment

You need three services running so you can verify the firewall rules actually work.

**Terminal 2 — Web application (port 8080):**
```bash
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

**Terminal 3 — Monitoring endpoint (port 9090):**
```bash
nc -lk 9090
```

Keep both terminals open and running throughout the lab. These simulate the real services the firewall will protect.

## Part 4: Setting the Default Policy and Enabling `ufw`

The default policy answers the question: *"What should happen to traffic that doesn't match any rule?"*

The secure baseline for any server is:
- **Block all incoming** — nothing gets in unless explicitly allowed
- **Allow all outgoing** — the server can freely reach the internet (for updates, API calls, etc.)

### Step 1: Allow SSH First (Most Important Step)

```bash
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-1.png)

> **Do this before anything else.** Once the default `deny incoming` policy is set and `ufw` is enabled, all unmatched traffic is blocked immediately. If SSH isn't allowed before that moment, you will be locked out of the server.
>
> Think of it this way: **always prop open the door you're standing in before you change the lock.**

### Step 2: Set the Default Policies

```bash
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
```

| Policy | What It Means |
|--------|--------------|
| `deny incoming` | All inbound connections are dropped unless a rule explicitly allows them |
| `allow outgoing` | All outbound connections are permitted unless a rule explicitly denies them |

### Step 3: Enable the Firewall

```bash
sudo ufw enable
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-2.png)

`ufw` will warn you that enabling it may disrupt existing connections. Since you already allowed SSH in Step 1, your session is safe. Confirm when prompted.

### Step 4: Verify the Firewall Is Active

```bash
sudo ufw status verbose
```

You should see:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-3.png)

The firewall is now live. Only SSH (port 22) is open — everything else is blocked.

## Part 5: Adding Allow and Deny Rules

Now that the firewall is active, let's open the specific ports the scenario requires.

### Step 1: Allow the Web Application (Port 8080)

The web app should be accessible to anyone on the internet:

```bash
sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp
```

Check the updated ruleset:

```bash
sudo ufw status numbered
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-4.png)

The `numbered` output assigns a number to each rule — you'll need these numbers later when deleting rules.

### Step 2: Allow the Monitoring Endpoint — Internal Network Only (Port 9090)

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/ufw-03.svg)

Before writing this rule, you need to know the internal network subnet. Run:

```bash
ip addr show
```

Look for the WireGuard interface (`wt0`) in the output:

```bash
5: wt0: <POINTOPOINT,MULTICAST,NOARP,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1280 ...
    inet 100.84.125.66/16 brd 100.84.255.255 scope global wt0
```

Two things to read from this line:
- The interface IP is `100.84.125.66`
- The `/16` subnet mask means the network range is `100.84.0.0/16`

The monitoring tool should only be reachable from within the platform's internal network (`100.84.0.0/16`):

```bash
sudo ufw allow from 100.84.0.0/16 to any port 9090
```

This rule enforces **two conditions simultaneously**:
1. The source IP must be within `100.84.0.0/16`
2. The destination port must be `9090`

Any connection to port 9090 from an IP outside that range will be silently dropped by the default deny policy.

Check the updated ruleset:

```bash
sudo ufw status numbered
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-5.png)

### Step 3: Explicitly Deny an Insecure Service (Port 23 — Telnet)

Even though Telnet would already be blocked by the default deny policy, adding an explicit deny rule is good practice:

```bash
sudo ufw deny 23/tcp
```

**Why bother if it's already blocked by default?**

- It documents the *intent* — future administrators know Telnet was consciously blocked, not just forgotten
- It survives if someone changes the default policy
- Security audit tools recognize explicit deny rules as a deliberate hardening decision

### Step 4: Review the Complete Ruleset

```bash
sudo ufw status numbered
```

Your ruleset should now look like this:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-6.png)

This matches the scenario's requirements exactly.

## Part 6: Deleting Rules

Stale firewall rules that are no longer needed are a security risk — they leave access paths open that should be closed. Always clean up rules when they're no longer required.

There are two ways to delete a rule:

### Method 1: Delete by Rule Number

First, find the rule number:

```bash
sudo ufw status numbered
```

Then delete using that number:

```bash
sudo ufw delete <rule-number>
```

`ufw` will ask for confirmation before deleting. This is intentional — there's no undo.

### Method 2: Delete by Rule Description

You can also delete a rule by describing it the same way you created it:

```bash
sudo ufw delete deny 23/tcp
```

This approach is safer when rules have been added or removed and the numbers may have shifted.

### Verify After Deletion

```bash
sudo ufw status numbered
```

Confirm that the deleted rule is gone and all remaining rules are exactly as expected.

## Part 7: Application Profiles

Remembering port numbers for every service is error-prone. `ufw` solves this with **application profiles** — named presets that map a service name to its ports and protocol.

Profiles are stored as files in `/etc/ufw/applications.d/` and are installed automatically when you install common packages like Nginx or OpenSSH.

### Step 1: See What Profiles Are Available

```bash
sudo ufw app list
```

Common profiles you'll see on Ubuntu:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-7.png)

### Step 2: Inspect What a Profile Contains

```bash
sudo ufw app info OpenSSH
```

Output:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/47dc4f840af146a6d75d022c4ed4348cfc86da88/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2018/images/image-8.png)

The `OpenSSH` profile is exactly equivalent to `ufw allow 22/tcp` — just named instead of numbered.

### Step 3: Allow a Service by Profile Name

```bash
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
```

Using profile names makes your ruleset more readable and maintainable. If a service ever changes its port (rare, but possible), you only need to update the profile file — all systems using `ufw allow <AppName>` automatically pick up the change.

## Part 8: Resetting and Disabling `ufw`

### Temporarily Disable (Rules Are Preserved)

```bash
sudo ufw disable
```

This stops the firewall immediately but keeps all your rules saved. Run `sudo ufw enable` to restore enforcement with the same ruleset.

**Use this when:** You need to temporarily stop the firewall for testing without losing your configuration.

### Full Reset (Rules Are Deleted)

```bash
sudo ufw reset
```

This disables `ufw` and wipes all rules. Before deleting, it saves a backup of your current rules to `/etc/ufw/*.rules.YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS` so you can recover them if needed.

**Use this when:** You want to start completely from scratch.

## Conclusion

You started with a completely open server and locked it down to exactly what the scenario required — no more, no less.

Along the way, you learned how to set a deny-all default policy, allow only the right ports to the right people and use application profiles instead of memorizing port numbers. The core rule to take away from this lab: **allow SSH first, block everything by default, then open only what you need**. Every port you don't open is an attack surface that doesn't exist.
